items.q: In a story about building a troubleshooting checklist, what most makes you sound like an engineer?
choices: Saying the checklist was very long
Explaining how you ordered the steps and the expected reading for each check
Mentioning that you laminated it
Saying your manager liked it
items.why: Ordering logic (quickest, most likely, or safest check first; splitting the system) and pass/fail values are the same design decisions as in a test procedure. That's the engineering content.

choices: "I had to do stuff with the checklist."
"The plant needed better documentation."
"I decided to make the fix repeatable, so the night shift could clear the fault without calling me in."
"My job was maintenance."
items.why: It states your responsibility, that you took the initiative, and what success looks like. The others are either vague or about the company rather than you.

items.q: You wrote one section of a team-written procedure. How should you tell it?
choices: Say you wrote the whole procedure
Say "I wrote the section on the conveyor faults" and describe that section in depth
Don't use this story
Say "we" throughout
items.why: A precise, honest scope is still a strong story, and it holds up under follow-up questions. Overclaiming is the fastest way to lose credibility.

items.q: Which Result is strongest for this story?
choices: "The checklist was finished and posted on the cabinet."
"Callouts for that fault dropped from roughly weekly to about once a month, and the night shift used it on their own."
"Everyone said it was great."
"It was very helpful."
items.why: It has an honest, roughly quantified change and evidence of adoption. Finishing a document isn't a result; what changed because people used it is.

items.q: How does a troubleshooting checklist relate to a pytest suite?
choices: They are unrelated
Both are ordered checks with expected values and pass/fail outcomes; pytest runs its checks automatically on every change
pytest only checks formatting
A checklist is only for hardware, so the skills don't transfer
items.why: Expected value, actual value, pass or fail, then what to do on failure: same structure. Saying this out loud in an interview is a strong bridge from maintenance to test engineering.

interview.q: Tell me about a time you created a process or a checklist that other people used.
rubric: Specific motivating problem, with the before state and what it cost
Explains how the checklist was built: sources of information, the logic behind the order of steps, and expected values or pass/fail criteria
Tested or reviewed it with someone else and revised it based on what happened
Concrete, honest result: repair time, repeat faults, callouts, or adoption
Clear personal role, and a bridge to test procedures, documentation, or robotics debugging

interview.q: Why would your maintenance background make you good at test and validation work?
rubric: Names transferable skills concretely: systematic diagnosis, measurement, documenting procedures, reliability thinking
Draws the parallel between troubleshooting checklists or PM tasks and test procedures with pass/fail criteria
Backs the claim with a short real example rather than general statements
Mentions current technical work that shows the bridge (for example sensor logging, pytest, or the IMU and motor test rig projects), without overclaiming
Confident and concise (under about 90 seconds), with no apologizing for the non-traditional background
